common_name: Ace of Spades Sweet Potato Vine (Spade-Shaped Near-Black Foliage Vine)

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or nursery starts once the soil has warmed after the last frost, in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; the pointed, spade-shaped leaves darken most dramatically where the plant gets several hours of direct sun.

directions: Ace of Spades bears distinctly pointed, angular leaves that echo the shape of a spade playing card, emerging medium green and quickly darkening to a deep purple-black as they mature in sun. Stems trail vigorously over container edges and hanging baskets, and the plant is equally effective massed as a warm-season groundcover under taller tropicals. Grow in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; a little afternoon shade in the hottest climates keeps the foliage from looking stressed without dulling its dark color. Pair with chartreuse or silver companions to make the angular black foliage read as a strong focal note in mixed plantings.

common_name: Sweet Caroline Purple Sweet Potato Vine (Compact Deep Purple Ornamental Vine)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; like the rest of the NC State-bred Sweet Caroline series, Purple was selected for a more restrained, manageable habit than older ornamental sweet potato vines.

directions: Sweet Caroline Purple carries deeply cut, finely serrated leaves in a rich, saturated dark purple that reads nearly black in strong sun and softens to plum in lower light. It rounds out the Sweet Caroline series alongside Bronze and Light Green, sharing the same compact, well-branched habit that stays tidier in mixed containers than older, more rampant sweet potato vine cultivars. Grow in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; it tolerates heat, humidity, and short dry spells once established, needing only occasional pinching to keep it proportionate to companion plants. The deep purple foliage is a reliable dark anchor color for combining with silver, chartreuse, or bright orange and pink flowering annuals.

common_name: Sweet Caroline Sweetheart Red Sweet Potato Vine (Heart-Leaf Multicolor Ornamental Vine)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; the Sweetheart sub-series was bred with smooth, unlobed heart-shaped leaves rather than the deeply cut foliage of the original Sweet Caroline introductions.

directions: Sweet Caroline Sweetheart Red produces smooth, unlobed heart-shaped leaves that shift through a blend of lime, wine, and bronze tones rather than settling into a single solid color, giving the vine a shifting, multicolor effect through the season. Its compact, well-branched habit trails more modestly than older sweet potato vine cultivars, making it a good fit for hanging baskets, window boxes, and the edges of raised beds without swamping neighboring plants. Grow in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; full sun intensifies the wine and bronze coloring, while some afternoon shade keeps the lime tones brighter in hot climates. It also performs well as a low, weed-suppressing groundcover when planted directly in the border.

common_name: Sweet Georgia Bronze Sweet Potato Vine (Compact Bronze Ornamental Vine)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Sweet Georgia Bronze stays much lower and denser than older ornamental sweet potato vines, making it well suited to small pots and tight edging.

directions: Sweet Georgia Bronze forms a dense, low mat of deeply lobed leaves in warm coppery bronze, staying noticeably shorter and tighter than the classic sprawling ornamental sweet potato vines like Margarita or Blackie. Its restrained scale makes it a practical choice for small mixed containers, window boxes, and front-of-border edging where a full-sized vine would quickly overwhelm its neighbors. Grow in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; it holds its bronze color best with several hours of direct sun but still performs respectably in brighter part shade. Trim lightly through the season only to keep the mounded shape neat.
sources: Green Fuse Botanicals plant introduction notes

common_name: Bright Ideas Black Sweet Potato Vine (Compact Maroon-Veined Black Ornamental Vine)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Bright Ideas Black keeps a bushier, more compact profile than heirloom dark-leaved sweet potato vines, needing less frequent trimming to stay in scale.

directions: Bright Ideas Black bears deeply cut, lobed leaves in rich dark purple-black with contrasting maroon veining, giving the foliage more visible texture and depth than solid-black cultivars like Blackie. The dense, bushy, trailing habit fills out mixed containers and hanging baskets quickly while staying more compact than older sweet potato vine selections, so it is less likely to overrun neighboring plants by midsummer. Grow in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; the darkest color develops with several hours of direct sun, though the plant remains vigorous in brighter shade positions. Use it as a dramatic dark filler or spiller against bright chartreuse or silver companions.

common_name: Bright Ideas Rusty Red Sweet Potato Vine (Compact Copper-Red Ornamental Vine)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; the Bright Ideas series was bred for a denser, more compact form than standard ornamental sweet potato vine, so Rusty Red needs only light shaping through the season.

directions: Bright Ideas Rusty Red carries deeply cut, lobed leaves in olive-green washed with warm rusty red-orange along the lobes and veins, a coppery two-tone effect distinct from the solid burgundy or near-black tones of most dark sweet potato vine cultivars. Its compact, mounding-to-trailing habit stays proportionate in small containers and hanging baskets rather than sprawling widely like older selections. Grow in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; the rusty coloring intensifies with more direct sun exposure. The warm copper tones combine especially well with orange, gold, or deep red flowering annuals in a mixed planting.

common_name: Sidekick Black Sweet Potato Vine (Well-Mounded Dark Purple Ornamental Vine)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Sidekick Black forms a well-mounded plant rather than sprawling flat, so it needs less frequent trimming to keep a tidy shape in containers.

directions: Sidekick Black produces star-shaped, deeply lobed, dark purple-black leaves on a semi-compact plant that mounds up before trailing, giving it more visible structure than flatter-growing dark sweet potato vine cultivars. The restrained, well-branched habit makes it an easy filler in mixed containers, window boxes, and hanging baskets without needing constant pinching back. Grow in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; it holds up well to heat and short dry spells once established, and the tuberous roots are drought tolerant. Combine with bright chartreuse, silver, or warm orange companions to set off the dark, star-patterned foliage.
